# Quantile {#sec-quantile}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
You are a genius!
:::

It is quite common to see on social media about a puzzle or equation which the reward that you will be a genius if you solve it, harvard entry exam, or 99% cannot solve this problem.
Those are meant to show that if you solve it, you are not unique but you are a member of a certain exclusive group.
While these post on social media probably has little source on how they get those numbers, the numbers are made up to make it sensational and grap one's attention, there is still underlying scientific/statistical reasoning behind it.

So how do we get the 99% cannot solve it, or equivalently, only 1% can only solve it.
The short answer is that someone asked say 1000 persons to solve a problem and only 10 solved. That means you belong to the top 1%.
The longer answer is that we extrapolate that your smartness (IQ) is above the 99% quantile. That is, if we order the IQ of the 100 persons from lowest to the largest, your IQ will be in the top 10 highest.

More generally, we can rank some values from the smallest to the largest. For any stop  you can always calculate how many is below and how many is above. What happens in general is that we pick the quantile and find the value of x where split the numbers in the given proportion. The most famous quantile is the mean, where half of the number are smaller than the median, and half of them are bigger.

## Formal {.unnumbered}
**Add interqualite range**

The concept of a quantile generalizes the median. While the median splits a distribution into two equal halves (50%), quantiles split a dataset or a probability distribution into arbitrary fractions or proportions, p (where 0<p<1).
Like other structural descriptors, its definition splits between sorting sample data in applied statistics and evaluating inverse functions in theoretical statistics.

1. Applied Statistics: The Sample Quantile
In applied statistics, the pth quantile (often called a percentile when expressed as a percentage) is a value that separates the lowest p fraction of the ordered data from the rest.
Textbook Source

Book: Statistics for Business and Economics (14th Edition, 2020)
Authors: David R. Anderson, Dennis J. Sweeney, Thomas A. Williams, Jeffrey D. Camm, and James J. Cochran
Publisher: Cengage Learning

The Definition
In Chapter 3 ("Descriptive Statistics: Numerical Measures"), the authors define the algorithmic process for finding the pth quantile (percentile) of a finite dataset:
"The pth percentile divides the data into two parts: approximately p percent of the observations have values less than the pth percentile, and approximately (100−p) percent of the observations have values greater than the pth percentile.
To calculate the pth percentile, first arrange the data in ascending order. Then determine the position index $L_p$:
$L_p = \frac{p}{100}(n + 1)$

where n is the number of observations."
(Note: If $L_p$ is not an integer, applied textbooks use linear interpolation between the two adjacent ordered values).

As this is the last chapter on basic, introduce more notation.

In other words, if the ordered observations are denoted
$x_{(1)},x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}$
​

Another definition is using CMF and CDF

## Examples {.unnumbered}
- Imagine a number 100 numbers: 1 to 50 and 1001 to 1050. The 1, 2, 3 % quantile is 1, 2 and 3 respectively, the 20% quantile is 20. The mediane is (50 + 1001)/2, the 51% quantile is 1001 and the 98 and 99% quantile is 1048 and 1049.

- Visualizing a quantile from distribution

```{r}
# Create data
# data_values <- rnorm(100)
# 1. Generate data
set.seed(42)
data_values <- rnorm(2000, 0, 10)

# 2. Calculate dynamic quantiles (7% and 75%)
q_low  <- quantile(data_values, 0.08) # ~ -13.8
q_high <- quantile(data_values, 0.75) # ~ +6.7

# 3. Calculate histogram object
my_hist <- hist(data_values, breaks = 40, plot = FALSE)

# 4. Dynamic color vector based on quantile midpoints
my_color <- ifelse(
  my_hist$mids < q_low, rgb(0.2, 0.8, 0.5, 0.6),
  ifelse(
    my_hist$mids >= q_high, adjustcolor("purple", alpha.f = 0.6),
    rgb(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2)
  )
)

# Expand bottom margin (mar[1]) slightly to accommodate extra x-axis labels
par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 4, 2))

# 5. Plot Histogram
plot(
  my_hist,
  col = my_color,
  border = FALSE,
  main = "Histogram with 8% and 75% Quantile Cutoffs",
  xlab = "",  # Suppress default xlab to avoid overlap with quantile values
  xlim = c(-40, 40),
  las = 1
)

grid(col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# Re-draw histogram bars over grid
plot(my_hist, col = my_color, border = FALSE, add = TRUE)

# 6. Add Vertical Bar Lines at Quantiles
abline(v = q_low,  col = "#0e6b38", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = q_high, col = "purple",  lty = 2, lwd = 2)

# 7. Add Labels at the top (Quantile names ONLY)
y_max <- max(my_hist$counts)

text(
  x = q_low, y = y_max * 0.95,
  labels = "Q 8%",
  col = "#0e6b38", font = 2, pos = 2, cex = 0.85
)

text(
  x = q_high, y = y_max * 0.95,
  labels = "Q 75%",
  col = "purple", font = 2, pos = 4, cex = 0.85
)

# 8. Add Quantile Numerical Values Below the X-Axis
# Redraw custom colored tick marks & values at quantile positions
axis(side = 1, at = round(q_low, 2), labels = round(q_low, 2),
     col.axis = "#0e6b38", col.ticks = "#0e6b38", font = 2, cex.axis = 0.85, line = -.75)

axis(side = 1, at = round(q_high, 2), labels = round(q_high, 2),
     col.axis = "purple", col.ticks = "purple", font = 2, cex.axis = 0.85, line = -.75)

# Add standard x-axis label shifted down to make space
mtext("value of the variable", side = 1, line = 3.8, cex = 0.9)

# Reset margin default
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)
```

The value of -10 represent x% and is the x% quantile, up to gray is x% quantile.
These are called quartile and is the 25% and 75% respectively.

```{r}
# 1. Generate data
set.seed(42)
N <- 2000
data_values <- rnorm(N, 0, 10)

# 2. Define Parametric Quantile Thresholds
p_low  <- 0.08  # 8%
p_high <- 0.75  # 75%

q_low  <- quantile(data_values, p_low)   # ~ -14.05
q_high <- quantile(data_values, p_high)  # ~ +6.70

# 3. Compute initial histogram without plotting
hist_object <- hist(data_values, breaks = 40, plot = FALSE)

# Convert counts to cumulative percentages (%)
hist_object$counts <- cumsum(hist_object$counts) / N * 100

# 4. Color vector based on bin midpoints (mids) matching cumulative thresholds
my_color <- ifelse(
  hist_object$mids < q_low, rgb(0.2, 0.8, 0.5, 0.6), # Below 8%
  ifelse(
    hist_object$mids >= q_high, adjustcolor("purple", alpha.f = 0.6), # Above 75%
    rgb(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2) # Between 8% and 75%
  )
)

# Expand bottom margin for quantile tick labels below x-axis
par(mar = c(6, 4.5, 4, 2))

# 5. Plot Base Cumulative Histogram
plot(
  hist_object,
  main = paste0("Cumulative Histogram with ", p_low * 100, "% and ", p_high * 100, "% Quantiles"),
  xlab = "",
  ylab = "Cumulative Percentage (%)",
  xlim = c(-40, 40),
  ylim = c(0, 105),
  col = my_color,
  border = FALSE,
  las = 1
)

grid(col = "gray90", lty = "dotted")

# Re-draw bars over grid
plot(hist_object, col = my_color, border = FALSE, add = TRUE)

# Percentage y-values for intersections
y_low_pct  <- p_low * 100
y_high_pct <- p_high * 100

# 6. Add Horizontal Segments (From left y-axis boundary at x = -40 to intersection point)
segments(x0 = -40, y0 = y_low_pct,  x1 = q_low,  y1 = y_low_pct,  col = "#0e6b38", lty = 3, lwd = 1.8)
segments(x0 = -40, y0 = y_high_pct, x1 = q_high, y1 = y_high_pct, col = "purple",  lty = 3, lwd = 1.8)

# 7. Add Vertical Segments (From x-axis baseline at y = 0 to intersection point)
segments(x0 = q_low,  y0 = 0, x1 = q_low,  y1 = y_low_pct,  col = "#0e6b38", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
segments(x0 = q_high, y0 = 0, x1 = q_high, y1 = y_high_pct, col = "purple",  lty = 2, lwd = 2)

# 8. Add Intersection Points & Labels
# Draw solid points at exact intersection coordinates
points(c(q_low, q_high), c(y_low_pct, y_high_pct),
       col = c("#0e6b38", "purple"), pch = 19, cex = 1.2)

# Quantile labels placed near intersection points
text(
  x = q_low, y = y_low_pct + 4,
  labels = paste0("Q ", y_low_pct, "%"),
  col = "#0e6b38", font = 2, pos = 2, cex = 0.85
)

text(
  x = q_high, y = y_high_pct + 4,
  labels = paste0("Q ", y_high_pct, "%"),
  col = "purple", font = 2, pos = 2, cex = 0.85
)

# 9. Add Quantile Numerical Values Below X-Axis
axis(side = 1, at = round(q_low, 2), labels = round(q_low, 2),
     col.axis = "#0e6b38", col.ticks = "#0e6b38", font = 2, cex.axis = 0.85, line = -1.)

axis(side = 1, at = round(q_high, 2), labels = round(q_high, 2),
     col.axis = "purple", col.ticks = "purple", font = 2, cex.axis = 0.85, line = -1.)

# Add main x-axis title shifted down
mtext("Values", side = 1, line = 3.8, cex = 0.9)

# Reset margin defaults
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2) + 0.1)

```

To compute quantile from cumulative distribution, we just project from left values and see the interesection from x axis.

## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}
- Computing the quantile can be ordered (see first calculation of the mean) or accumalted frequency (visualization from distribution).
- Median is the 50% quantile
- The interquartile range is the value between 25% and 75% and is another way of representing the dispersion of a distribution. It is used in boxplot.
- the p-value is a quantile. For two sided test, a p-value at 5% represent values below the 2.5% and 97.5% quantile. (although we did not talk anticipate). For one side, a 5% could be 5% below that or above 95%.
- The quantile is approximated if there is not enough data (e.g. ). Such approximation might be meaningless.
